slides.text:
One DSD People, Access and Culture
Person-Centered Thinking in Public Decisions
Keep people’s goals, preferences, and chosen support visible in the forms, guidance, and decisions that shape daily life.
Foundation self-directed learning
slides.narration: A public decision can affect someone’s week long before the staff member writing it meets that person. A form, instruction, service category, or development option can make some possibilities visible and others harder to pursue. Person-centered thinking helps you examine that connection. This course uses service, workplace, and community examples to practice listening and decision reasoning. You will keep the person’s purpose visible while retaining actual responsibilities, real limits, and questions that require more information than the example supplies.

slides.text:
What is lost when a goal becomes a category?
A person wants to create pottery with a friend. A note reduces this to “attend an activity weekly.”

Attendance may occur while friendship and creative choice remain absent.

What information would help you understand what the activity means to the person?
slides.narration: The attendance description is not necessarily false, but it is incomplete. The person’s purpose includes a relationship and a way to create, not only a place on a calendar. If that meaning disappears from the record, staff may compare options only by whether an activity occurs. Repeating that shortcut can make service categories more visible than people’s lives. Ask what a satisfying experience would involve and retain the answer. You need not promise the requested arrangement to take its meaning seriously.

slides.text:
Begin with the life, then consider support
Person-centered thinking starts with the person’s goals, interests, relationships, strengths, and preferences.

Supports are considered in relation to that life rather than replacing it.

General respectful practice does not grant assessment, funding, or formal planning authority.
slides.narration: The starting question changes what staff are able to see. Asking which service fits may produce a useful administrative answer while leaving the person’s reason unexplored. Asking what matters can make the later comparison more meaningful. Both the goal and the actual options remain important. This introductory course prepares that reasoning; it does not qualify someone as a formal planner or authorize a service. Keep the appropriate process intact while examining how ordinary questions and documents carry the person’s meaning.

slides.text:
A form can choose the starting point
A draft form asks people to select a service before describing what they want their week to include.

People may shape their answer around the menu. Repeating the form can make unfamiliar goals disappear.

Consider a goal-first question while retaining information the actual process needs.
slides.narration: Forms are conversations designed in advance. Their first questions can signal which answers the organization expects. A service-first menu may be necessary at some point, yet it can make people translate their lives into categories before anyone understands the purpose. The next choice asks how to improve that starting point without discarding required information. A revised question is a proposal that needs appropriate review. It does not establish a new entitlement or guarantee that every desired arrangement becomes available.

slides.text:
Let the goal enter the form
A draft form asks people to select a service before describing what they want their week to include. Which revision best supports a person-centered conversation?
A. Remove every required question and promise any desired service.
B. Keep only the service list because personal goals are too varied to matter.
C. Include a goal-first question and retain necessary service information for appropriate review.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.
slides.narration: The form needs to support its real administrative purpose while making the person’s life visible. A service category can be useful later in the conversation, but asking only for a category may cause people to narrow their answer before staff understand the goal. Compare a revision that opens inquiry with one that removes responsibilities or assumes personal meaning is irrelevant. The form does not supply actual required fields, eligibility, or funding rules. Your response should prepare an appropriate review rather than claim an approved service decision.

links.name: Answer 1
links.text: A. Remove every required question and promise any desired service.

links.name: Answer 2
links.text: B. Keep only the service list because personal goals are too varied to matter.

links.name: Answer 3
links.text: C. Include a goal-first question and retain necessary service information for appropriate review.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
Removing requirements and promising options without authority can mislead people. Respect the goal while retaining actual processes. Repeated overpromising can damage trust; this draft does not establish eligibility or available funding.

What would your goal-first question help staff understand?
Continue learning
Try another response
slides.narration: A desired life deserves serious attention, but it does not remove actual program requirements. Promising every requested arrangement may create expectations that staff cannot meet, especially if repeated through a standard form. Keep the goal visible and explain the real decision process. The learning case supplies no authority to remove requirements and no evidence that a particular service is available or appropriate.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
A menu-only conversation can make the system’s choices the whole goal. Repetition may hide interests outside familiar categories. Ask what matters before comparing options; the person’s purpose is not yet known.

What would your goal-first question help staff understand?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: The service menu answers an organizational question while leaving the person’s purpose unexplored. Repeating that starting point can make unfamiliar goals hard to express and steer plans toward what the system already provides. Add an appropriate question about what matters while retaining necessary information. The person’s actual interests and the effect of a revised form remain unknown until they are considered.

slides.text:
Why this response helps
This makes the person’s purpose visible alongside needed information. It may interrupt a recurring menu-first default. Use appropriate review and keep real limits clear; the answer does not authorize a service.

What would your goal-first question help staff understand?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: The revision makes the goal part of the conversation without pretending that the answer settles eligibility or resources. It can help staff compare options by the experience the person wants, rather than only by category. Appropriate content review and actual planning responsibilities remain. The proposed question is a supported learning step; no approved form or improved service outcome is supplied.

slides.text:
Important to and important for belong together
What matters to the person includes relationships, routines, interests, and experiences.

Relevant health, safety, and support needs remain part of the conversation.

Ask how a specific concern can be addressed without making the goal disappear.
slides.narration: A desired life and an identified support concern should not be treated as competing sides that can only defeat one another. A person may want a community activity and also want information about an unfamiliar route. Name the particular concern rather than using a vague safety label to close inquiry. Dismissing the concern also fails to support an informed choice. The appropriate roles can consider information and support together. This course does not assess an actual risk or replace the responsibilities that apply in practice.

slides.text:
Understand strengths before adding instruction
A person may bring knowledge, skills, relationships, and experience that the service category does not describe.

Ask what is already familiar and what support would be useful now.

Do not require someone to prove basic readiness again because the goal is unfamiliar to staff.
slides.narration: In the pottery example, the person may already understand design and color mixing. Automatically assigning basic instruction could replace the creative goal with a lesson they did not need. The same issue can appear when staff presume an employee needs beginner training before hearing about prior experience. Ask relevant questions and consider the evidence appropriate to the activity. Repeated readiness assumptions may delay opportunity. Recognizing strengths does not settle every support need; it helps make the next inquiry more accurate.

slides.text:
A meaningful choice needs useful information
Options may share a label while offering different experiences, costs, supports, or availability.

Explain what is known, what differs, and what remains uncertain.

A yes-or-no answer after staff select the option is not the whole choice conversation.
slides.narration: Two activities called pottery might involve making with a friend or watching a demonstration alone. The broad label hides the difference that matters to the person. Describe relevant features clearly and distinguish available arrangements from possibilities needing inquiry. Do not present an unknown as a guaranteed approval or a familiar service as the only direction worth considering. A useful comparison supports understanding within real limits. The person may choose differently from staff, and the account should leave room for that response.

slides.text:
Chosen support can strengthen the person’s voice
A person may want privacy, time to think, or conversation with someone they choose.

Support does not automatically replace their position; choosing alone is not the only form of agency.

Ask how the person wants others involved and use appropriate information arrangements.
slides.narration: People learn different meanings of independence and mutual support. Someone may value deciding privately, while someone else exercises control by discussing options with a trusted friend. Neither preference should become a profile of a whole community. Ask about the role the chosen person should have and retain the individual’s own position. A support person’s suggestion is not automatically the final choice. Relevant legal authority and information-sharing responsibilities remain distinct from the learning example and should follow the actual process.

slides.text:
A development plan chosen before the conversation
A supervisor selects a learning path before asking about the employee’s goals. The employee wants a different area of practice.

The preselected path may obscure interests and strengths. Repeating it can narrow development opportunity.

Compare the goals, work needs, and realistic options together.
slides.narration: Person-centered thinking can inform a supportive employee conversation without turning supervision into service planning. The employee’s interests matter alongside role expectations and available opportunities. A preselected path may fit some needs, but staff should understand what it misses before calling it the appropriate development plan. The next case asks how to compare those considerations without promising unlimited options. The fiction does not establish the employee’s complete goals, all organizational constraints, or the effect of a later choice.

slides.text:
A development path chosen too soon
A supervisor selects the team’s usual course before asking about an employee’s goals and prior experience. The employee wants another area of practice. What response is most useful?
A. Compare the employee’s goals, work needs, prior experience, and realistic learning options.
B. Require the usual course because identical paths prove fairness.
C. Guarantee the employee’s preferred option before checking what it offers or what is available.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.
slides.narration: A supervisor can value an employee’s interests while keeping role expectations and organizational needs clear. The usual course might still be useful, but its familiarity does not establish that it fits this person’s development. Consider what each option offers, what the employee already knows, and which constraints are real. A collaborative comparison is different from either imposing sameness or promising every preference. The fiction does not supply the final decision, all available resources, or the employee’s later experience, so those remain questions rather than assumed outcomes.

links.name: Answer 1
links.text: A. Compare the employee’s goals, work needs, prior experience, and realistic learning options.

links.name: Answer 2
links.text: B. Require the usual course because identical paths prove fairness.

links.name: Answer 3
links.text: C. Guarantee the employee’s preferred option before checking what it offers or what is available.

slides.text:
Why this response helps
This connects listening with relevant work standards and actual options. It may reduce a recurring default that narrows development. Clarify the comparison; suitability, availability, and later learning effects are still unknown.

Which difference between the options would matter for this employee’s work?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: This comparison gives the employee’s account a meaningful place in development while retaining actual work needs. Prior experience may change which learning is useful, and available options may differ in what they offer. If repeated, this approach can interrupt a default that overlooks people’s strengths. It does not guarantee the preferred course, establish approval, or prove a later improvement in work; those need their own evidence.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
Identical paths can overlook different experience and goals. Repetition may distribute learning opportunities poorly. Examine the task and relevant criteria; sameness alone does not establish fairness or useful development.

Which difference between the options would matter for this employee’s work?
Continue learning
Try another response
slides.narration: A common standard can be important without requiring an identical path for everyone. Automatically using the same course may ignore prior experience or a different relevant learning need. If sustained, that habit can narrow who develops which capabilities. Compare options against actual work criteria and the employee’s goals. The practice case does not establish that the usual course is unsuitable, only that its fit has not been examined.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
An unchecked guarantee can mislead and bypass relevant responsibilities. Take the goal seriously while examining fit and availability. The case does not establish approval or that the preferred option meets the work need.

Which difference between the options would matter for this employee’s work?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: Taking an interest seriously does not require a guarantee before relevant information is known. The option may have practical limits or offer something different from what the employee expects. An unchecked promise can damage trust when it cannot be delivered. Explain the inquiry and compare fit honestly. Availability, approval, and the eventual development effect remain outside the information supplied by this case.

slides.text:
The employee life cycle contains chosen directions
Onboarding, feedback, assignments, and development can make room for a person’s goals and prior experience.

Consistent work standards need not mean identical learning paths.

Ask what a relevant option offers rather than relying only on what the team has used before.
slides.narration: Employees can pursue the same work standard through different learning experiences. Someone entering a role may need an introduction, while someone with relevant experience may benefit from a more focused opportunity. Later development can connect personal interests with organizational needs. The actual criteria and available arrangements still matter. Repeatedly using the same familiar path without inquiry may distribute opportunity poorly. This is a question to examine in the specific setting, not a claim that every difference in training proves unfairness.

slides.text:
Follow a decision into the person’s day
A deadline, proof request, contact route, or instruction can become someone’s practical task.

Ask what the person must do to use the decision and what resources it assumes.

The person may not be in the drafting room, but their experience can still inform review.
slides.narration: A paragraph can become a trip, a call, a document request, or a wait in someone else’s day. State-system work often encounters that consequence indirectly, through guidance and procedures. Trace the relevant sequence rather than imagining care ends when the wording is approved. A step may assume transport, internet access, time, or institutional familiarity. Those assumptions need examination, not automatic rejection. Appropriate evidence and affected people’s accounts help clarify whether the decision functions as intended and which questions remain open.

slides.text:
Prepare for varied meanings without profiling
Community briefs can help staff notice different histories and meanings of family, support, and choice.

Use them to prepare open questions, not to predict an individual.

People affected by a process can explain how it works in their daily lives.
slides.narration: A brief may help you recognize that your preferred form of choice is not universal. It should not make you decide what an individual wants based on a community label. Ask a question that leaves the person free to explain or decline. Engagement can bring varied experience into review, including consequences staff do not encounter themselves. Repeatedly hearing only familiar perspectives may keep one default unquestioned. Preparation supports a more informed conversation while the person’s own meaning and actual process remain central.

slides.text:
Participation needs an open question
Explain what people can influence and which limits are real.

A request for feedback after every meaningful choice is settled may collect experience without using it.

Invite relevant knowledge without asking community members to do staff’s whole analysis.
slides.narration: People can contribute practical knowledge without taking over the organization’s responsibilities. A clear question explains what is being considered and what cannot change through that conversation. If the only available contribution is agreement, calling the activity open can damage trust. Staff can still hear concerns about a settled arrangement, but should say honestly how that information may be used. Person-centered thinking values the account while retaining decision roles. It does not promise that every recommendation will become the final choice.

slides.text:
A notice assumes that one route fits every week
A draft notice requires a daytime in-person response. A participant explains how work and transport make that route difficult.

Ignoring the account can make a routine administrative step a recurring barrier.

Examine the purpose, real requirements, and possible response alternatives.
slides.narration: The participant identifies how a written decision reaches daily life. Their account can make an assumed resource or schedule visible. Staff need to examine the notice’s purpose and actual constraints, rather than dismiss the experience or promise an exception without authority. A culture brief may prepare relevant attention, but this particular account supplies the practical concern. The next choice asks how to use it within an appropriate review. It does not establish the best alternative or every affected person’s circumstances.

slides.text:
A notice reaches into daily life
A draft notice requires a daytime in-person response. A community participant explains difficulties involving work and transport. Which response best uses that account?
A. Dismiss the concern because the notice is the same for everyone.
B. Examine the purpose, actual requirements, and usable alternatives through appropriate review.
C. Publish the participant’s story as proof that the notice harms everyone in their community.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.
slides.narration: The participant’s account identifies a practical effect that may be hard to see from the drafting room. A daytime visit can become a transport arrangement or time away from work. Those conditions matter without automatically deciding that the requirement is invalid or that a particular alternative must be offered. Consider which response makes the account useful to an appropriate review. A community brief can prepare questions, but it cannot expand this one account into every person’s experience. No approved change or public sharing permission is supplied.

links.name: Answer 1
links.text: A. Dismiss the concern because the notice is the same for everyone.

links.name: Answer 2
links.text: B. Examine the purpose, actual requirements, and usable alternatives through appropriate review.

links.name: Answer 3
links.text: C. Publish the participant’s story as proof that the notice harms everyone in their community.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
Sameness can preserve different burdens. Repeating the route may exclude people who cannot use that time and place. Examine the actual step and account; identical wording does not establish equal access.

What does the account reveal about the notice’s assumed resources?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: The same instruction can require different effort depending on people’s schedules and resources. Treating identical wording as proof of equal access leaves that practical difference unexplored. If repeated, the route may make completing a routine step harder for some people. Examine the actual requirement and possibilities through the responsible process. The participant’s account identifies a concern; it does not establish every affected person’s experience.

slides.text:
Why this response helps
This connects the instruction with daily experience while retaining real requirements. It may reveal a recurring burden staff can address. Check alternatives appropriately; the best response and wider effects remain unknown.

What does the account reveal about the notice’s assumed resources?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: This option carries the person’s experience into the decision without erasing the notice’s purpose or promising an unauthorized exception. The review can ask whether the time and place are necessary and what usable alternatives exist. That may address a repeated burden. The suitable response still needs information and appropriate review, and no later change or improvement is established in the fiction.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
One account cannot establish a universal effect, and public use needs appropriate permission. Repeating overgeneralization can profile a community. Keep the practical concern and scope clear; broader experience is unknown.

What does the account reveal about the notice’s assumed resources?
Continue learning
Try another response
slides.narration: Publishing a story and claiming universality go beyond the supplied information. The participant may not have agreed to public use, and others may encounter the notice differently. Repeating that shortcut can turn useful engagement into profiling. Preserve the practical question, use appropriate information arrangements, and seek other perspectives where needed. The case leaves broader experience, permission, and the final notice decision open.

slides.text:
A completed plan and a meaningful experience differ
A plan written, visit held, or service delivered describes activity.

The person’s account helps explain whether the experience moved toward what mattered to them.

Mixed results can be informative; do not ask for a positive answer to justify staff effort.
slides.narration: The pottery visit might occur and produce an object while leaving little time with the friend. Those facts can coexist. Attendance matters to the activity record, but it does not answer the relationship question. Ask how the experience fit the person’s purpose without leading the answer. A person may value part of the arrangement and want another part changed. Keeping that distinction visible helps review the actual support. It does not establish that staff effort lacked value or that the whole plan failed.

slides.text:
A changed goal is information, not noncompliance
Preferences and circumstances can change as a person learns from experience.

Ask what the new direction means before treating it as refusal or inconsistency.

Actual requirements remain, and the appropriate process considers what can change.
slides.narration: Someone may discover that an activity is different from what they expected or that another goal now matters more. The change can clarify their desired life rather than prove they were never serious. Repeatedly treating revised preferences as a problem may lock people into arrangements that no longer fit. Hear the account and explain real limits accurately. The responsible process still governs actual decisions. A learning conversation can prepare a better question without determining an entitlement, authorization, or agreed next step.

slides.text:
Rewrite a system-first question
Choose the service form, development plan, or notice.

Write a question that makes the person’s purpose visible while retaining necessary work information.

Explain what the answer could change and what it could not decide.
slides.narration: Try changing the starting point without removing the task’s purpose. “Which service do you want?” might be accompanied by a question about what the person wants their week to include. A development conversation might ask which work the employee hopes to deepen before comparing available options. State how the answer informs review and what remains governed by the actual process. Your reflection can remain private. The aim is an understandable connection between the person’s meaning and the decision, not an unlimited promise.

slides.text:
Listen after the action
A proposed question, approved change, and later experience are different parts of the account.

Seek relevant feedback and keep missing information visible.

No later reply does not establish agreement, goal achievement, or a reason to close inquiry.
slides.narration: A changed form may invite a more meaningful answer, but you still need information about how it works for people. A revised plan may reflect an agreed direction while leaving the actual experience ahead. Distinguish these stages clearly. Feedback can show an improvement, a remaining barrier, or a changed preference, and its scope should remain honest. Avoid making the person certify success to reward staff effort. Continued attention respects their agency and helps the system learn without claiming more than the evidence supports.

slides.text:
Carry the person’s meaning into the decision
Person-centered thinking connects goals, chosen support, useful information, and attention to daily experience.

Keep real limits and responsible processes clear while examining system defaults.

Continue with Charting the LifeCourse, self-direction, and equity review resources when they help.
slides.narration: The cases show that person-centered thinking is relevant even when the staff task is a form, a notice, or a development conversation. The person’s purpose can remain visible while actual responsibilities and constraints are respected. Compare options by what they offer in relation to that purpose. Listen after a change and leave room for new information. A more thoughtful question is a useful beginning, not a completed service decision. Continued learning helps staff carry care into the ordinary choices that shape people’s lives.

outcomes: Describe person-centered thinking in terms of a person’s goals, preferences, and chosen support.
Trace how a form, instruction, or internal decision can affect daily life.
Distinguish a choice meaningful to the person from a choice defined solely by available services.
Ask how the person’s voice can inform a decision within the responsible staff member’s role.
